source: LLM-based system for argument mining (arXiv 2605.13793, ICLR 2026 workshop, C4AI-USP)
finding: Ten-step GPT pipeline turns text into an argument graph: premises, conclusions, support, attack, undercut. It has an explicit step that classes premise groups as linked or convergent, and a step that adds implicit premises.
numbers: Models GPT-4.1, GPT-5, GPT-5-mini. Own dataset: 42 short arguments from an argumentation textbook (Sacrini 2023).
limits: Linked premises are modelled as an empty intermediate node that joins them. This adds nodes. Authors say it gives a more accurate structure at the cost of more nodes.
agent_relevance: Direct template for S2: a join node for linked premises, none for convergent ones.

source: LLM-based system for argument mining (arXiv 2605.13793, ICLR 2026 workshop, C4AI-USP) - component level
finding: On textbook arguments, conclusion detection was very accurate; span detection was weaker because the model merged sentences the gold diagram split.
numbers: Conclusion detection accuracy 92.50%. Span detection precision 80.31, recall 72.87, F1 75.70. Relation accuracy 80.57% (only arguments with at least 2 matching components).
limits: Single annotator. Gold diagrams allow several valid splits. Failed when the conclusion was implicit: the system could not handle it.
agent_relevance: Expect the conclusion to be found; expect span boundaries and implicit conclusions to be the weak point in S1.

source: LLM-based system for argument mining (arXiv 2605.13793, ICLR 2026 workshop, C4AI-USP) - structure and global ratings
finding: Two annotators rated implicit premises, undercuts, linked/convergent grouping, completeness and faithfulness on a 1-3 scale. All rated very good.
numbers: Implicit premises M=2.86 (exact agreement 0.95). Undercuts M=2.90 (0.88; only 8 arguments had undercuts). Linked/convergent M=2.85 (0.80). Completeness 2.96 (0.97). Faithfulness 2.92 (0.88).
limits: Short textbook arguments, lenient 3-point scale, alternative readings accepted, no kappa reported. Undercut judging often rested on counterfactual reasoning.
agent_relevance: Linked vs convergent had the lowest rating and lowest agreement. Treat that label as the least trusted part of a diagram.

source: LLM-based system for argument mining (arXiv 2605.13793, ICLR 2026 workshop, C4AI-USP) - external benchmarks
finding: On public corpora with exact span matching the full pipeline did badly. With gold components it was much better, so the bottleneck is finding spans, not relating them.
numbers: AbstRCT: span F1 59.65 (full) vs 70.93 prior best (Morio 2022); link F1 20.82 (full) vs 51.51 with gold components (prior best 39.74). AAEC: full pipeline link F1 0.41; with gold components about 22.88 (prior best 55.72).
limits: Exact-match spans punish LLM paraphrase. AAEC essays are long. Pipeline not tuned to the benchmark schema. Table columns garbled in PDF extraction, so AAEC column assignment is uncertain.
agent_relevance: Give the agent the units; do not ask it to cut text spans and link them in one pass. Segment first (S1), link second (S2).

source: Gupta, Zuckerman, O'Connor (2024) Harnessing Toulmin's theory for zero-shot argument explication (ACL 2024)
finding: Prompting a model with 'According to Toulmin model' makes it output claim, grounds and warrant. Plain prompts ('What is the claim?') give paraphrase and extra material.
numbers: Success rate (all three terms present), ARCT/MCT: GPT-4 99.0/100.0, GPT-3 94.6/95.4, Llama-2-70B 75.2/90.2, Falcon-40B 35.0/42.5. Generic open prompts gave on-topic components in only 38.39%, 24.10%, 21.42% of responses.
limits: Success rate counts term presence, not correctness. Small datasets (ARCT, MCT).
agent_relevance: Naming the schema in the prompt is a cheap S2 move. Check slot presence first, then content.

source: Gupta et al. (2024) - human check of generated warrants
finding: Hidden-premise (warrant) quality: GPT-4 warrants were judged acceptable more often than the datasets' gold warrants. Llama-2-70B was far worse.
numbers: 300 judgments per warrant type: gold 45.7% acceptable, GPT-4 61.7%, Llama-2-70B 26.3%. Annotator agreement low: kappa 0.18 gold, 0.24 GPT-4, 0.31 Llama-2. BERTScore to gold 0.2-0.4.
limits: Two annotators, low kappa, so warrant acceptability is subjective. Generated warrants differ from gold, so overlap metrics mislead.
agent_relevance: A strong model can state the hidden premise, but each warrant still needs a second check given the subjectivity.

source: Gupta et al. (2024) - prompt wording and theory choice
finding: 'Toulmin model' was the best of the name variants. References to Toulmin beat references to Walton schemes and Freeman structure in all four models.
numbers: C4 mentions: Toulmin 3401, Walton 975, Freeman 66. Authors link success to how often the theory appears in pretraining text.
limits: Correlational. Only ARCT used for the theory comparison.
agent_relevance: Prefer the best-known schema name (Toulmin) over a more exact but rare one when prompting.

source: Glockner, Hou, Nakov, Gurevych (2024) MISSCI: Reconstructing Fallacies in Misrepresented Science (ACL 2024)
finding: Dataset of fallacious arguments reconstructed from fact-checks. The model must write the hidden fallacious premise and name the fallacy. GPT-4 beat Llama 2 70B but premise generation stayed weak.
numbers: 208 misrepresented-publication links found (Krippendorff alpha 0.728); 153 arguments reconstructed by all assigned annotators. GPT-4 found at least one fallacy (P@1) in 57% of arguments. Arg@6 reached 89.0% (GPT-4) and 59.7% (Llama 2). Human check of 240 outputs: NLI-S metric correlated best with humans (Pearson r=0.209).
limits: Health-misinformation domain. 4-bit Llama 2 and a 2023 GPT-4. Automatic premise metrics correlate weakly with humans.
agent_relevance: Reconstructing a hidden premise is much harder than classifying the fallacy once the premise is given. Make S2 write the premise out, then judge it.

source: MISSCI - prompt content effect
finding: Fallacy definitions (D), logical forms (L) or examples (E) changed classification and premise writing differently. Definitions alone gave the best fallacy class; logical forms gave the best premise text.
numbers: With the gold premise given, classification is strong (9-way task). Without it, GPT-4 improves when it also writes its own premise; Llama 2 does better without writing one. Models over-predicted False Equivalence; Ambiguity vs False Equivalence confused. Llama 2 never predicted Ambiguity or Impossible Expectations.
limits: Prompt picked on 30 validation arguments. Few examples per class.
agent_relevance: Writing the missing premise first, then labelling the gap, helped the stronger model. A weak model gets worse from writing premises.

source: Chen, Cheng, Luu, Bing (2024) Exploring the Potential of Large Language Models in Computational Argumentation (ACL 2024)
finding: Zero-shot and few-shot tests of GPT-3.5-Turbo, Flan models and Llama-2 on 14 argumentation datasets (11 mining datasets in the zero-shot table). The small Llama often falls below random.
numbers: 500 sampled examples per dataset. GPT-3.5 and Flan-UL2 beat random on most; Llama-2-13B fell below random on most, notably FEVER stance and evidence classification. Under 10 demonstrations matched models fine-tuned on 500 samples.
limits: 2023-era models. Mostly sentence-level classification, not full diagrams.
agent_relevance: More shots help bigger models; smaller models do not gain. Examples are a lever, not a guarantee.

source: Abkenar et al. (2024) Assessing Open-Source Large Language Models on Argumentation Mining Subtasks
finding: Four open models on argumentative unit classification (ADUC) and relation classification (ARC) across three corpora. Demonstrations stabilise rather than lift. Context-aware prompts help weak models and can hurt strong ones.
numbers: 3-shot AMT1: Llama3 86% with plain prompt but 61% with context-aware prompt; Llama2 48% to 63% with context-aware prompt. LLMs matched or came close to prior best micro-F1 on AMT1 and PE for ARC; worse on AMT2.
limits: Small open 2024 models; some figures only in charts. Microtext and persuasive essays only.
agent_relevance: Extra context in the prompt is not free: it can lower a strong model. Test, do not assume.

source: Pietron et al. (2026) A comprehensive study of LLM-based argument classification: from Llama through DeepSeek to GPT-5.2
finding: Argument relation classification on UKP and Args.me with ten models. Best model GPT-5.2. Rephrasing the prompt four ways and voting raised accuracy; self-rated certainty was unreliable.
numbers: GPT-5.2 accuracy 78.0% (UKP) and 91.9% (Args.me). Voting gain over baseline: UKP +4.4 (simple), +4.5 (tie-break), +2.4 (certainty-weighted) points; Args.me +2.6, +2.8, +2.9. Natural-language answer formats beat symbolic ones on average. Spread across prompts typically 2-4 points.
limits: Pair classification (support/attack/neutral), not whole-diagram construction.
agent_relevance: Cheap robustness: ask the same link question several ways and vote. Do not weight by the model's own stated certainty.

source: Pietron et al. (2026) - chain-of-thought result
finding: Chain-of-thought was tried only on Llama models (others have built-in reasoning). The effect was mixed.
numbers: Gains of a few points for larger models; the paper calls efficacy mixed.
limits: Only Llama family; I did not read the exact table.
agent_relevance: CoT is not a reliable gain for link classification. Voting was steadier.

source: Ajjour, Quensel, Lipka, Wachsmuth (2026) ArgBench: Benchmarking LLMs on Computational Argumentation Tasks
finding: 33 datasets, 46 tasks, five skills (mining, perspective, quality, reasoning, generation), eleven LLMs from five families. Few-shot (4 examples) was best for models of 32B or more.
numbers: Mean few-shot F1 on perspective assessment 0.486. Zero-shot size gain largest for mining (+0.037 to +0.102 macro) and perspective (+0.033 to +0.078). Argument quality assessment was the hardest skill. CoT beat zero-shot on quality for all but Llama-3.1-8b and GPT-4.1, but was near zero-shot on reasoning for Llama, Mistral, Qwen3.
limits: Prompting only; 4 random examples; DeepSeek-R1-32b did not gain from few-shot. Includes warrant-generation tasks.
agent_relevance: Large models: use about 4 examples. Reasoning models: do not add few-shot. Test CoT per sub-task.

source: ArgBench - cross-task transfer
finding: Fine-tuning on other argument skills transfers weakly. Training on the same skill as the target works best.
numbers: Argument similarity: quality-skill training beat all-task training (0.541 vs 0.468).
limits: LoRA on one 22B model (Mistral); limited tasks.
agent_relevance: Do not expect a skill taught in one argument task to carry over; build the scaffold per sub-step.

source: de Wynter & Yuan (2024) I'd Like to Have an Argument, Please: Argumentative Reasoning in Large Language Models (COMMA 2024)
finding: GPT-3 and GPT-4 on argument mining (BIO tags) and argument pair extraction. Same task wording, different input/output format changed scores a lot. Authors conclude the models do not reason reliably about arguments.
numbers: RRv2 data (474 test pairs). Concrete prompts: GPT-3 AM 39.86, GPT-4 64.51; APE 18.58 and 53.84. Symbolic (indices): GPT-4 AM 70.63, APE 49.85. GPT-4 beat the best prior APE system by 14 points F1. Binary-matrix output gave 9.88 F1, below random. Peak at about 4 exemplars, then decline.
limits: Only review/rebuttal text. 2023 GPT-3/4. 'Cannot reason' is the authors' reading of format sensitivity.
agent_relevance: Fix an output format (line numbers, short labels) and keep it fixed. Format changes alone move scores by tens of points.

source: de Wynter & Yuan (2024) - CoT and abstraction
finding: CoT was robust to format changes but its outputs were similar across formats. Without CoT, more abstract input (graphs, AMR) lowered scores but stayed above random.
numbers: Welch t-test: with CoT, line numbers vs BIO tags made no difference (p about 0.77); without CoT p < 0.05.
limits: A template-like CoT may just fix the format. Exemplar-count effect did not extend further.
agent_relevance: A fixed step-by-step template makes output format stable.

source: Castagna, Sassoon, Parsons (2024) Critical-Questions-of-Thought: Steering LLM reasoning with Argumentative Querying
finding: Agent loop that uses Toulmin: the model writes a plan as premises and conclusions, answers 8 critical questions mapped to Toulmin parts, repeats until at least 7/8 are yes, then answers.
numbers: Up to 5 tries needing 7/8 yes, then 5/8, max 10 tries. MT-Bench reasoning and math, 5 models, LLM judge, mean score 1-10. CQoT best in 18 of 20 comparisons plus joint best in one. Llama 3.1-70B reasoning: standard 8.05, CoT 7.5, CQoT 8.4. Nemotron-51B reasoning: standard 6.75, CoT 7.7, CQoT 7.3 (CQoT worse than CoT).
limits: Small test, LLM judge (GPT-4o / Claude 3.5 Sonnet), free-tier models, no human check, authors' own method. Claude 3.5 Sonnet: CoT and CQoT equal on math.
agent_relevance: Toulmin used inside an agent loop with a pass threshold. Matches an S2-then-check loop, but gains are small and unproven at scale.

source: CQoT - ablation
finding: Dropping the critical-question steps (keep plan and answer only) scored lower than the full loop but still above the plain baseline.
numbers: Llama 3.1-70B reasoning: standard 8.05, steps 1+4 8.3, full 8.4; math 8.95, 9.25, 9.55. Nemotron-51B reasoning 6.75, 6.85, 7.3; math 8.75, 9.0, 9.15.
limits: Two models only. Means with no significance tests.
agent_relevance: Much of the gain may come from writing the premise-conclusion plan itself; the questions add a smaller part.

source: Feng & Hunter (2026) Making Implicit Premises Explicit in Logical Understanding of Enthymemes
finding: An LLM writes intermediate premises, they are turned into logic (via AMR), and an entailment check is run. More generated steps gave higher entailment accuracy; one generated premise beat the dataset's own premise.
numbers: 250 entailment items per setting. ANLI accuracy: none 0.496, original 0.520, 1-step 0.624, 2-step 0.660, 3-step 0.716. ARCT: 0.276, 0.292, 0.480, 0.496, 0.560.
limits: Candidates are fixed (two per item), so it tests classification, not free premise generation. Low absolute ARCT accuracy. Thresholds tuned per dataset.
agent_relevance: Hidden premises can be chained: each added bridging premise improved the logical link. Still verify with a separate or symbolic check.

source: Feng & Hunter (2026) Identifying Implicit Premises for Logical Reconstruction of Argument Graphs
finding: Same pipeline applied to arcs of the Microtext argument graphs, three classes (entail, contradict, neutral). Accuracy rose as implicit-premise steps accumulated, peaking at four.
numbers: Accuracy 0.426 with no implicit premise, 0.512 with one, 0.555 at 4 steps; chance 0.333.
limits: Premise-claim pairs only; Microtext is short, simple text; best thresholds picked on the same data.
agent_relevance: Supports adding bridging premises in S2, with a limit: step 5 added nothing.

source: Wang, Ma, Yin, Ma, Malone (2026) Graphionale: How Graph Visualizations of LLM Rationales Affect Human Decision Making (UIST 2026)
finding: An LLM prompt turns a rationale into an argument map (premises, sub-conclusions, conclusions, support and objection edges). The map was built reliably. In a human study the graph helped on hard verbal tasks but felt worse to use.
numbers: 180 rationales: only 5 structure faults (2.8%). Wrong-answer rationales: wrong sub-conclusion 30/60, bad evidence 26/60, missing evidence 10/60. N=204 (Prolific). Verbal (BBH) hard items: over-trust down (b=-0.199, p=.002), error correction up (b=+0.182, p=.002); no effect on easy items. Visual (I-RAVEN) reversed.
limits: Humans read the map; the model did not use it. Benefit limited to hard verbal items and high need-for-cognition users.
agent_relevance: Making inference steps explicit exposes wrong sub-conclusions; our agent can check them mechanically.

source: Li, Schlegel, Sun, Batista-Navarro, Nenadic (2025) Large Language Models in Argument Mining: A Survey
finding: Survey up to Sept 2025: argument mining moved from task-specific classifiers to prompting, retrieval and reasoning-oriented approaches. Notes risk of bias and circularity when an LLM helps annotate and an LLM is then tested.
numbers: Notes GPT-4 proposing evidence spans in machine-in-the-loop annotation (ASE corpus). No headline number used here.
limits: I read only the abstract, taxonomy and annotation parts; no numbers extracted.
agent_relevance: Datasets differ in annotation scheme, so scores across papers are not comparable.

source: Bhatia & Parent (2026) Guided Sensemaking: Agents in Collaborative Deliberation
finding: System paper: a Reflector agent extracts claims, premises, support and attack into a discourse graph so reasoning stays visible. No outcome numbers in the parts I read.
numbers: None reported in the parts read.
limits: Prototype; I read only the introduction and design sections.
agent_relevance: Example of an agent loop that stores arguments as a graph rather than as chat text.

source: Mori et al. (2026) WarrantScore: Modeling Warrants between Claims and Evidence for Substantiation Evaluation in Peer Reviews
finding: A metric where an LLM writes the implicit warrant linking claim and evidence in peer-review comments, then a classifier scores its acceptability. Reported to correlate better with human scores than claim-evidence-presence methods.
numbers: Evaluated on RottenReview (753 review comments, 5-point Likert, Spearman). Warrant-acceptability classifier trained on 450 warrants with human labels.
limits: Spearman values not extracted by me. Peer-review domain only.
agent_relevance: The warrant gets its own check: a separate classifier judges whether the hidden premise links grounds to claim.
